transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-03-02 14:00 PT — Duration ~48m. Attendees: Alex Park (Redwood AE), Nina Rao (Redwood SE), Daniel Brooks (CTO, Lumenova), Maya Singh (SRE Lead), Ethan Cole (ML Eng).

Summary: Quick readout of week-two bench results vs their incumbent, focused on tail latency during burst, a routing tweak Nina prototyped, and decisions around canary vs full roll. We hit an unexpected tail spike at ~95th–99th percentile on certain 512-token prompts; team discussed KV cache warmup and fallback to smaller quantized model. Action items captured.

Topics: bench deltas vs incumbent, tail-latency root causes, routing playbook (latency vs cost), canary thresholds, next head-to-head.

00:00 Alex (AE): All right everyone, uh good afternoon — thanks for joining. Quick check, audio ok?
00:08 Daniel (CTO): Yeah we can hear you, thanks. Busy week but excited to see numbers.
00:13 Nina (SE): Morning from my side — I pushed the new routing policy to the lab cluster last night, it's the one that favors hosted-capacity first, then falls back to quantized dedicated.
00:24 Maya (SRE): Noted, we saw that. We also rolled your instrumentation change for prefix cache, so we've better traces now.
00:33 Alex: Cool. Quick agenda: Nina will walk the bench diffs, then we talk tail-latency, then routing decisions.
00:40 Nina: Great. Slide-free, I'll just share my screen after this — but high level, week two we've got steady throughput improvement — p99 is still the pain point. For median and p50-perf we beat IncumbentAI by about 18% on token throughput at the same slot config. However, p95/p99 on some 512 token flows spiked to ~720ms which is above your tolerance.
01:10 Ethan (ML Eng): Just to add — those 512 requests are mostly our long-form summarization endpoint which uses context windows and a few retrieval calls. There's some extra pre and post processing which sometimes blocks the inference threads.
01:25 Maya: There's also bursts — we replicated E2E load with the same burst pattern you sent, and the tail moves quite a bit. We suspect K-V cache cold start and the first-token overhead.
01:40 Nina: Right, K-V cache warmup for large sequences — plus the runtime does a kernel switch at sequence length thresholds; that switch causes that micro-jitter, it's more visible under burst. Some of the kernel handoff is actually an artifact of how we choose GEMM kernels for long seq.
02:00 Alex: Can you explain the kernel switch in non-engineering terms for Daniel?
02:05 Nina: Sure — think of it as the engine changing gears when an input hits a length bucket. Most of the time it's seamless, but under bursts we see a 2–3ms microskip escalate because of resource contention so it pops into the p99. Also prefix cache miss makes the first token slower.
02:25 Daniel: So it's not an algorithmic slow path, it's a warmup/hand-off problem?
02:28 Nina: Exactly, mostly warmup and resource scheduling. There's also a small amount of serialization in your preproc that eats inference concurrency.
02:40 Ethan: That preproc is intentionally single-threaded for dedupe safety; we can try parallelizing it but want to measure correctness risk.
02:50 Maya: For now we care about mitigation strategies — what did you try?
02:53 Nina: Two immediate levers: aggressive prefix caching to reduce first-token cost, and fallback routing to a low-cost quantized variant when predicted latency risk is high. We also tried bumping the warm-pool reserve sizes so that there's a smaller cold pool.
03:10 Alex: What's the delta when you enable aggressive prefix caching?
03:13 Nina: Median doesn't change much, but p95 drops from ~380ms to ~220ms in the lab for the 256-token flows. For 512s, p99 improves from ~720ms to ~410–430ms. Not perfect but better.
03:30 Maya: Those numbers look promising. How reproducible are they?
03:34 Nina: Reproducible in the lab under replicated traffic for two of three runs; the third run had a tail outlier which we traced to a background host DST that kicked in — noisy neighbor.
03:50 Daniel: Curious about cost impact. Aggressive caching — does that blow up token cost?
03:55 Nina: Minimal. The extra memory pressure is negligible on our instance sizes. You trade a small memory footprint for much better token-level latency. The routing fallback to quantized option reduces unit cost by ~28% for those requests that hit fallback, but quality is slightly lower — we evaluated BLEU/ROUGE-ish style deltas for your comparator prompts, it's within your QA tolerance for nontop-k-critical tasks.
04:20 Alex: Okay, talk to me about routing policy. We have an approach that predicts latency risk from request features and routes accordingly — what's the current threshold?
04:28 Nina: We're using a heuristic that uses request token count, retrieval count, and a rolling host-load metric. If predicted 95th > 500ms we route to quantized fallback or to a dedicated warm slot. The canary config we pushed uses 10% canary to quantized fallback and 90% to primary.
04:50 Maya: We ran that canary and saw mixed results — the canary split helped reduce p99 overall but we saw increased error rate on long-form outputs when quantized hit. Some of that is our QA checks which are strict.
05:08 Daniel: So decision is tradeoff between our success metric and saving cost. We need to keep user-perceived QA above 98% pass.
05:17 Nina: Understood. One other thing — we found IncumbentAI is doing a similar fallback but they prefer aggressive model-slicing which costs them on throughput. In our runs we still maintain higher tokens/sec than IncumbentAI even with fallback enabled.
05:36 Alex: Let's play out a scenario: 5 minute burst to 3x baseline, what happens?
05:42 Nina: With conservative warm-pool and fallback we see median hold and p95 increase by ~40% but p99 stays under 800ms. Without fallback, p99 can climb to 1.1s depending on noisy neighbor occurrence.
06:00 Maya: That's a big difference. Can you do an automated fallback rule that looks at rolling p95 and flips at runtime?
06:07 Nina: Yes — we have a policy engine that can toggle fallback when rolling p95 crosses 450ms for 60s. We can tune the window.
06:17 Ethan: Any revert safety? We want auto reverting to avoid oscillation.
06:20 Nina: We built hysteresis — it requires p95 to be below 380ms for 90s before flipping back. It reduced oscillation in our lab runs.
06:34 Daniel: Good. About the head-to-head — what should we expect when we run IncumbentAI?
06:38 Alex: We'll run identical traffic, same preproc, same retrieval patterns. Nina will instrument both and we'll measure median/p95/p99 and unit cost. We'll pick a few representative prompts including the 512-token ones.
06:50 Maya: For logs we'll share the tail traces and the exact request IDs. Expect us to mask PHI; it's synthetic but modeled on your production shape.
06:58 Nina: Also note we ran a quantized 4-bit variant in lab — quality delta on your set was a 1.2% drop on the metrics you sent, which you earlier said was acceptable for internal summarization.
07:14 Daniel: Right, external facing patient-facing summ maries cannot drop; internal summaries ok. We'll need routing to preserve model quality for patient-facing endpoints.
07:24 Alex: So simple plan: configure route rules by endpoint tag — patient-facing routes never go to quantized fallback unless explicit override by ops. Internal ones can fallback.
07:36 Maya: That helps. How hard is it to tag endpoints?
07:39 Ethan: We already have metadata field in our API gateway, it's trivial — we can send the tag map.
07:44 Nina: Great. We'll wire the routing rule to that tag.
07:48 Alex: Any security/compliance notes from last week?
07:51 Daniel: We're still waiting on the SOC2 appendix for your dedicated offering. Procurement has flagged it.
07:57 Alex: Got it — I'll push the latest SOC2 appendix and the private deployment diagram post-call.
08:02 Nina: One more perf note — the kernel handoff we discussed earlier shows up in CPU-side traces as context-switch bursts; we have a micro patch that avoids a synchronous barrier and it's reduced p99 by ~60ms in lab. We'll include that in the next image for your lab cluster.
08:16 Maya: Would that require a restart window?
08:19 Nina: Rolling restart, no downtime — 10–15 minute rolling across pods.
08:23 Daniel: Fine. Schedule maintenance window if needed.
08:27 Alex: Recap of decisions: 1) Enable aggressive prefix cache and warm-pool bump in the lab; 2) Use routing playbook with endpoint tag to avoid quantized fallback for patient-facing; 3) Run head-to-head with IncumbentAI next week; 4) SE to push kernel micro-patch to lab image; 5) Lumenova to provide 48h tail logs.
08:48 Nina: I'll push the playbook JSON and canary config after this call to the shared drive, link is in the meeting notes.
08:54 Ethan: Quick Q — can we test the routing thresholds in a canary region first? We prefer staging before lab-wide.
09:00 Nina: Yes, I'll scope a region-level canary and include a rollback plan.
09:06 Daniel: Sounds good. Anything else?
09:09 Alex: No, that's it. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the head-to-head invite and final playbook.
09:17 Maya: Thanks.

End of call.

Notes and references: shared drive: /redwood/lumenova/poc/playbooks/routing-v2.json (Nina uploaded); benchmark sheet: https://redwood.sheets/ops/lumenova-week2 (view only).

Key numbers called out: median tokens/sec +18% vs Incumbent; p95 improvement with caching 380->220ms (256 tokens); p99 for 512 tokens improved 720->410ms with caching + warm-pool. Quantized fallback reduces unit cost ~28% for routed requests with ~1.2% quality delta on internal set.
notes: Meeting ended with concrete canary plan and head-to-head scheduled
